---
title: "The For Loop"
unit: 2
cluster: "Collections and Repetition"
---

A list can contain many values. Selecting and using each value by its index
would repeat the same code. A `for` loop performs the same work for every
element in a list.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to:

* write a `for` loop
* use the loop variable
* identify the indented loop body
* follow the order in which a loop runs

**A `for` loop runs an indented block of code once for each element in a
collection.**

## A loop over a list

Suppose a list contains three language names:

```{python}
languages = ["Python", "Shell", "Markdown"]
```

This loop displays every element:

```{python}
for language in languages:
    print(language)
```

The loop uses the elements in the order in which they appear in the list.

The first line has four parts:

| Part | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `for` | starts a loop |
| `language` | the loop variable |
| `in languages` | takes values from `languages` |
| `:` | marks the start of the loop body |

The name `language` is singular because it refers to one element at a time.
The name `languages` is plural because it refers to the complete list.

## How the loop runs

Python takes the elements from `languages` in order:

1. `language` refers to `"Python"`, and the body displays `Python`.
2. `language` refers to `"Shell"`, and the body displays `Shell`.
3. `language` refers to `"Markdown"`, and the body displays `Markdown`.

Each run of the loop body is called an **iteration**. This loop has three
iterations because the list has three elements.

The loop variable can be used in an expression:

```{python}
marks = [72, 85, 91]
for mark in marks:
    print(mark, mark + 5)
```

On each iteration, `mark` refers to the next integer in the list. The loop
displays that integer and the result of adding `5`.

## The indented body

The spaces at the start of a line are called **indentation**. Indentation tells
Python which lines belong to the loop:

```{python}
for language in languages:
    print("Learning", language)
print("Done")
```

The first `print()` is indented, so it runs once for each element. The second
`print()` is not indented, so it runs once after the loop has finished.

Use four spaces for each level of indentation. Every line in the same loop
body must have the same indentation.

## Summary

| Form or rule | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| `for language in languages:` | starts a loop over `languages` |
| `language` | refers to one element during each iteration |
| `    print(language)` | an indented line that belongs to the loop body |
| `:` | marks the start of the loop body |
| four spaces | the indentation used for one level |
| an unindented line after the body | runs after the loop has finished |

And the one idea to carry forward: a `for` loop visits each element in order
and runs the indented body once for that element.
